categoryCoverage.note: release() is correctly restricted to beneficiary; there are no owner/admin roles or other privileged functions in this contract.
No price or rate oracle is read anywhere in this contract.
No flash-loan interface or lending-protocol interaction is present.
The single low-level call's boolean return value is checked via require immediately after the call.
vestedAmount() multiplies before dividing, which is the precision-preserving order; no division-before-multiplication pattern is present.

The missing-cumulative-tracking root cause (no state records the amount already released) also enables a same-transaction reentrant exploit via beneficiary's receive/fallback, but this shares SC02's invariant and remediation exactly (see F-58ed17be) rather than being a second, independent root cause: fixing the SC02 finding (update released before the transfer) closes this path too, so it is not reported as a separate finding here.
Solidity 0.8.20 applies default overflow/underflow checks, no unchecked blocks are used, and startTime cannot exceed a later block's timestamp.
No delegatecall, proxy structure, or upgrade entry point is present.

findings.description: vestedAmount() always returns the total amount vested since startTime, not the amount still owed, and release() forwards this full to-date figure on every single call instead of the incremental unreleased balance - the contract does not actually implement incremental vested-claim accounting (invariant violated: cumulative amount released must never exceed vestedAmount() minus what was already released). Even with a single, non-malicious beneficiary calling release() more than once as time passes - an ordinary way to interact with a vesting contract - the second call will try to resend the entire cumulative vested amount again, either reverting once the already-paid amount exceeds the remaining balance (permanently stranding the rest of the beneficiary's legitimately vested funds) or, if the contract holds surplus ETH, overpaying beyond the true entitlement. The same missing state update also means that if beneficiary is, or later becomes, a contract, its receive/fallback function can call release() again before the outer call returns and pass the identical check, letting a single transaction's worth of reentrant calls drain far more than what has actually vested - potentially the entire balance - in one shot rather than over several separate calls. Both paths share one root cause and one fix.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a released state variable, compute the newly claimable amount as vestedAmount() - released on each call, transfer only that delta, and update released before the transfer (checks-effects-interactions - this ordering is what also closes the reentrant path). Optionally apply a reentrancy guard as defense in depth.

findings.description: The constructor stores _beneficiary without checking it against address(0), and the contract provides no function to update beneficiary afterward. If it is deployed with the zero address by mistake, release()'s require(msg.sender == beneficiary) can never succeed for any real caller, so any ETH later sent to the contract through the payable receive() function becomes permanently unrecoverable, with no owner or rescue mechanism present anywhere in the contract.
findings.recommendation: Add require(_beneficiary != address(0), "zero beneficiary"); in the constructor.

limitations: Off-chain logic, deployment configuration and key management were not assessed.
Operational security, infrastructure and tokenomics outside the analyzed code were not assessed.
Deployed contract state and third-party systems were not assessed.

riskIndicator.explanation: This indicator reflects findings detected within the analyzed scope. It is not a measure of overall protocol security.
